read_from: The route text as served: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 306f3b285898, store_version 87b13b1169b4 (its index.json), for "Hebrew WordNet PWN 3.0 alignment bridged to Open English WordNet 2025 by complete permanent-sense-key agreement" (M57): 313 routes (axis: routes), 298 letters keys (axis: keys). The source audit (builder/02-audit.mjs, evidence about the source and no part of any test): the source is the Hebrew WordNet of the Open Multilingual Wordnet, bridged by permanent sense keys to Open English WordNet 2025, in ledgers/work/ldmprs/source-cache/omw-hebrew-pwn30-2026-07-14/ and ledgers/work/ldmprs/source-cache/open-english-wordnet-2025-2026-07-15/. Through the dictionary store's records every one of the 313 routes is tied to one synset, and the record's gloss equals the text after the bar on its line of the source's data file on 315 of 315 records. The route equals the source's whole gloss on 69 routes and is the gloss less its example sentences on 244; no route is anything else. In the source's own XML, all 45 of the 45 distinct texts that hold a semicolon stand in one Definition element, so a semicolon here does not join two of that file's definitions. So a route comes from one field and no test here stands on a guess about a field. The key on file: this release keeps the data-file form that the WordNet manual describes, and that manual stands in the first folder, in WordNet-3.0.tar.gz: doc/man/wndb.5, doc/man/wngloss.7 and doc/man/wninput.5. They say that each synset has one gloss, a text string that provides a definition of what the synset represents, example sentences, or both. They name no sign inside a gloss; a search of what they say on a gloss (builder/02-audit.mjs, source-audit/key-search.json) finds no line that names a comma, semicolon, colon, hyphen, slash, quotation mark, dash or ellipsis, and the round brackets they name are the ones the lexicographer's file puts round the whole gloss, which reach no route. The second folder holds this release's licence and manifests beside its data, and no line of them on a gloss or a definition names a sign. So every shape's meaning here begins "unverified:".

definitions.terms: In every test a character is one index of the JavaScript string: every route holds only characters of 16 bits. A letter is any character of Unicode category L (JavaScript \p{L}), of any script and either case. A digit is one of the ten characters 0 to 9. Whitespace is what JavaScript's String.prototype.trim removes, and trimmed means with that removed from both ends. The text is the whole route text as it stands, the field route of a line of the by-source JSONL, what the checker gives the classifier, and never the field def. The text before and the text after the mark are the template's c.before and c.after, never trimmed unless the test says so. What a bracket holds is the template's c.group, the same for an opener and for its closer, and it is not trimmed. Empty means no character at all. Directly before and directly after name the one character next to the mark; at an end of the text no character stands there, so a test that asks for a character there fails. A string stands between « and », which are not part of it, and a full stop after » belongs to the sentence. Every string and every list minds case and is matched exact to the character, and no test matches part of a string in a list. The apostrophe is the straight one, U+0027; the left single quotation mark is U+2018 and the right single quotation mark is U+2019; the hyphen is U+002D. No test uses a class of case. Two tests that compute a string: THE PIECE AFTER THE MARK: take the text after the mark; if it holds a comma or a semicolon, of any container, keep only what stands before the first of them; trim that; keep its first 40 characters, or all of it if it is shorter; do not trim again, so the result may end in a space. THE FIRST WORD: of a named text, the run of letters and digits that starts at its first character, empty if that character is neither a letter nor a digit or the text is empty; the first word after the mark is the first word of the trimmed text after the mark. IN A GRAMMAR LABEL, a test on a mark: the text before the mark holds a semicolon, and the first word of the trimmed text that stands after the last semicolon of the text before the mark is one of the strings in grammar_label_openers; if the text before the mark holds no semicolon the test fails.
definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order they stand in this file; the first whose test holds names the occurrence, and no later shape is tried for it. A shape's container field is not part of its test unless the test says so. An occurrence that no shape of its mark takes makes the classifier throw. Not caught above means the shapes listed above it for the same mark.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no entry number. The source tells two meanings under one Hebrew word apart by the synset's number, and the route store does not carry it; the dictionary store's record keeps it (its loc). The source's own files carry that id and the store dropped it. By the audit each text under a key comes from one synset, and on all 15 of the 15 keys with more than one text each text is a synset of its own (axis: keys; example key קרב). WordNet does not separate homonyms from senses: a synset is one meaning, however its words are related, so this count holds both.

branches.question: Some rows give two wordings of one meaning, with a semicolon or a comma between them: make a compromise; arrive at a compromise. In this dictionary a row is one meaning of the word, so by the source's own account the second wording offers no different meaning. No sign in the row can tell a second wording from a note, so these rows were picked by hand. Today the page never cuts at a semicolon, and it cuts at a comma where a piece is short. Should these marks cut the row? From the day this is wired, each of these rows prints whole unless you answer that they cut. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other question: no row stands under both, and each answer cuts only at its own marks.

options.means: The page prints each wording as a reading of its own: make a compromise and arrive at a compromise. It cuts only at these marks, and at no other mark of the same row. A word like or or also that opens a wording stays in it, and a note stays with the wording it stands beside, even where it speaks of both.
The page prints each row as one reading, as written: make a compromise; arrive at a compromise. For a row with a comma that the page cuts today, this is a change from today.

branches.question: One definition reads the end of a word, then in round brackets a suffix or inflectional ending or final morpheme. The bracket gives a second wording of the one meaning, and in this dictionary a row is one meaning of the word, so by the source's own account it offers no different meaning. No sign can tell it from a bracket that only narrows a wording, so it was picked by hand. Today the page never cuts at a round bracket and prints this row whole. Should this bracket cut the row? From the day this is wired, the row prints whole unless you answer that it cuts. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other question: no row stands under both, and each answer cuts only at its own marks.

options.means: The page prints the end of a word and a suffix or inflectional ending or final morpheme as readings of their own. It cuts at the opening bracket only, so the closing bracket stands at the end of the second reading until the page takes it off, and that is a step of its own that the page must add.
The page prints the row as one reading, as written, with its brackets.

not_done_here: This ledger leaves to the store every route that holds no mark, because a shape stands only at a mark, and every question of whether a row renders the word it is filed under; the 16 rows it names for this stand in rows-for-the-store-v1.jsonl, outside the shapes, as examples and no census, and nothing is struck. A note after a wording stays in that wording's piece under the answer divides, and a label on the word's grammar stays in its row under every answer, since version 1.1 has no piece for a note.
